A bit late, but I do have one question.
Why use the actual target size (physical/logical) instead of a range between 0 and 1? Most of the time this would probably be enough and there would be no need to update all cameras should the target size change, if all you want is to use for example half the screen:
Camera 1 Viewport -> offset (0.0, 0.0), size (0.5, 1.0)
Camera 2 Viewport -> offset (0.5, 0.0), size (0.5, 1.0)

This would simplify the user side. And if there's a need for the actual size, users could still query it.

I definitely considered this (and I'm still open to discussing it). The reason I didn't was that there are legitimate use cases for both approaches. Split screen will (generally) benefit from percentages. Minimaps will (generally) want absolute values. Given that absolute values are what the wgpu viewport abstraction uses, it felt better to provide direct access to that rather than extra converting back and forth.

Maybe we should provide both options!

Just two random cents, but the viewport size, could maybe be an enum, allowing for both percentage and absolute values, and likewise for the viewport position. I can definitely see the usecase for both at least. easier to handle scaling in a game or UI that way. 

I do not know the code complexity changes for this though...

> viewport size, could maybe be an enum, allowing for both percentage and absolute values, and likewise for the viewport position

This could be a nice follow-up PR. I'd be interested in exposing this as a more general-purpose API, similar to (or even merged with!) what we're doing with `Size` over in `bevy_ui`. Can you make an issue and link this conversation?

issue_context.title: Consider adding a viewport abstraction
issue_context.body:
This is related to #197 but didn't want to derail the original bug

Bevy has a window abstraction, basically HashMap<WindowId, Window>. I think we may want a viewport abstraction as well. The default behavior would be that a window has a single viewport that fills it completely. I could see this being useful for an editor where we might want to render two views of the same scene, or render a single view within just part of the window. (Likely with UI surrounding it) (Draggable UI panels might have their own viewports for example)

I would suggest setting it up as a separate resource that looks a lot like the Windows resource, but where each viewport has a WindowId indicating which window contains it. (HashMap<ViewportId, Viewport>, Viewport is a struct that contains a WindowId)

This could have some camera state to help with converting between 2D/3D (or just reference a camera that has that information).
comments: I'm trying to implement something like this in #1389 to scratch my own itch (windowless cameras). Feedback is definitely appreciated.

review_comments: Why `f64` here when we use `f32` basically everywhere else?
Winit uses f64 for the scale factor. Thats really the only reason.
This should note that 0 is the default priority, and explain why it's needed.

```suggestion
                // the bottom-left of our right-hand viewport should start in the center of the screen at the bottom
                physical_position: UVec2::new(window.physical_width() / 2, 0),
```
The origin is the top left (see my comment in the other thread).

I just want to note that this PR and specifically this example is something I wanted to be able to add debug meshes for view frusta and such so the debug mesh for one frusta is visible from another view. I think in general this will help me debugging stuff like the cascaded shadow maps. Maybe it was just meant to be that this PR would come first. ;)
Maybe rename this now the system name is being changed?
I tend to find that it's clearer to define components before using them, but that's just a matter of style.

In the case of examples, I like having "main" first, immediately followed by the "setup" function, then everything else. Main defines the high level context and setup defines the "scene layout", which seems worth prioritizing so users dont get lost in the weeds. Even in a non-example context this still makes sense to me because if we were to build a "split screen" plugin, we would extract out these components (and the system) and the diff wouldn't involve moving `setup` around.
Yeah, I don't feel strongly here :)
Buuut for really large / complicated setup functions, i see an argument for putting example-related components first / directly after main to ensure they get appropriate attention / don't get buried.
I think I prefer "to" over "into" here. I also like the flow of the original. "to which" feels a bit unnatural and formal to me.
As always, english grammar is polarizing :)

To be fair, I’m split in this internally. Ending sentences with prepositions is grammatically bad. But everyone commonly speaks and writes that way, which makes it more accessible and has a better tone. I always feel awkward saying ‘into which’ or whatever, and I’ve had to think ahead about the full sentence to know if it was necessary to be able to adjust and say it that way. Bleh. Happy to go along with honestly simpler language, even if my training also makes my brain poke me when I see prepositions at the end of sentences.

```suggestion
    /// Cameras with a lower priority will be rendered below cameras with a higher priority
    pub priority: isize,
```

```suggestion
                // bottom-left is (0,0) for both the window and the camera viewports
                physical_position: UVec2::new(0, 0),
```

Top-left is actually the origin in this case (same coordinate system as images). That point of clarity actually isn't directly relevant to this case, as both bottom-left and top-left code would look the same. I think I would argue that specifying that extra context makes this example less "minimal" than it could be.
I'm on board; I just saw that this information is included in the docs for `physical_position`.
Doc strings please; the use of this field is not immediately obvious to me.
The camera config could use a few more comments describing what's being done.
